title: Coulomb’s law
idea: The electric force between two point charges depends on their charges and the square of their separation.
variables: F is force in newtons; q₁ and q₂ are charges in coulombs; r is separation in metres. In vacuum k ≈ 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².
steps: Convert microcoulombs to coulombs: 1 μC = 10⁻⁶ C.
Square the distance in metres, then substitute into the formula.
The magnitude is positive. Like charges repel; opposite charges attract.
examplePrompt: For 1 μC and 2 μC separated by 0.20 m in vacuum:
pitfall: Use metres and coulombs before calculating.

title: Inverse-square scaling
idea: With both charges and the medium fixed, spreading the separation reduces force by the square of that change.
variables: r₁ and r₂ are the original and new separations. This relation assumes point charges, or a valid point-charge approximation.
steps: Write the distance multiplier first: r₂ = a × r₁.
Square that multiplier: the new force is F₁/a².
A larger separation gives a smaller force. No differentiation is needed.
examplePrompt: The separation doubles while both charges stay unchanged.
exampleSteps: r₂ = 2r₁, so F₂/F₁ = (1/2)².
F₂ = F₁/4. Halving the separation instead gives 4F₁.
pitfall: An inverse-square law is different from an inverse-distance law.

title: Quantisation of charge
idea: A body’s net charge comes in whole-number multiples of the elementary charge.
variables: Use the magnitude of Q to find the number of excess or missing electrons. The sign tells you which.
steps: Calculate n = |Q|/e.
A negative charge means excess electrons.
A positive charge means electrons are missing.
examplePrompt: A body has a net charge of −4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
exampleSteps: It has three excess electrons relative to its neutral state.
pitfall: Do not treat a negative net charge as a loss of electrons.

title: Adding electric fields
idea: The net electric field is the vector sum of the fields from each source charge.
variables: An electric field points away from a positive source charge and toward a negative one.
steps: Draw each field direction at the observation point.
Find the magnitudes using the distances to that point.
Add the signed components; equal opposite fields cancel.
examplePrompt: Two identical positive charges are equally far from their midpoint.
exampleSteps: At the midpoint, the left charge produces a field to the right.
The right charge produces an equally strong field to the left. The net field is zero.
pitfall: Magnitudes alone do not determine a vector sum.

title: Conservation of charge
idea: In an isolated system, charge can move between bodies but the total remains unchanged.
variables: Isolation means there is no transfer of charge to or from the surroundings.
steps: Add the initial charges algebraically, keeping their signs.
Touching may redistribute charge.
Report the total separately from the charge on an individual object.
examplePrompt: Two isolated conductors initially have +7 μC and −3 μC.
exampleSteps: Their initial total is +4 μC.
Their total after touching and separation is still +4 μC.
pitfall: Equal sharing requires extra symmetry conditions; conservation does not.

title: Force in a dielectric
idea: For fixed free point charges in a uniform dielectric, a higher permittivity reduces their electrostatic force.
variables: εr is the medium’s relative permittivity. Hold the free charges and separation fixed for this comparison.
steps: Find the relative permittivity.
Divide the vacuum force by that value.
Keep the original attraction or repulsion direction.
examplePrompt: A vacuum force is 0.8 N; the relative permittivity is 4.
exampleSteps: Fmedium = 0.8/4.
The new force magnitude is 0.2 N.
pitfall: The force is divided by relative permittivity, not multiplied.

title: Ohm’s law
idea: For an ohmic conductor at unchanged physical conditions, current is proportional to the applied voltage.
variables: V is voltage in volts, I is current in amperes and R is resistance in ohms. Keep temperature and other physical conditions fixed.
steps: Identify which of V, I and R is unknown.
Rearrange the equation before substituting.
For a ratio comparison at fixed R, I₂/I₁ = V₂/V₁.
examplePrompt: An 8 Ω resistor is across 16 V. The voltage later doubles.
exampleSteps: Initially I = 16/8 = 2 A.
At unchanged resistance, doubling voltage doubles the current to 4 A.
pitfall: Do not reverse V/R, and check that resistance is unchanged.

title: Resistors in parallel
idea: Parallel resistors share a voltage. Their branch currents add, so their equivalent resistance is smaller than the smallest branch resistance.
variables: Use reciprocal addition for parallel resistors. For two branches, Req = R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂).
steps: Confirm that both ends of each resistor share the same two nodes.
Add reciprocals, or use the two-resistor product-over-sum formula.
Take the reciprocal to recover resistance.
examplePrompt: 4 Ω and 12 Ω are in parallel.
exampleSteps: Req = 3 Ω, smaller than 4 Ω.
pitfall: Adding resistances directly is the series rule, not the parallel rule.

title: Electrical power in a resistor
idea: Electrical power is the rate of energy transfer. Choose the equivalent power formula that matches the quantities supplied.
variables: P is in watts. The resistor forms use V = IR.
steps: If I and R are given, use I²R.
If V and R are given, use V²/R.
Square the appropriate quantity before multiplying or dividing.
pitfall: IR is a voltage; it is not the power.

title: Resistance and wire geometry
idea: For a uniform wire of unchanged material and temperature, resistance increases with length and decreases with cross-sectional area.
variables: ρ is resistivity, L is length and A is area, not radius.
steps: Write each change as a multiplier.
Form the ratio R₂/R₁ = (ρ₂/ρ₁)(L₂/L₁)(A₁/A₂).
If radius changes, convert it into an area change using A = πr².
examplePrompt: Length triples and area doubles at fixed resistivity.
exampleSteps: R₂/R₁ = 3/2.
The new resistance is 1.5 times the original.
pitfall: Account for both geometry changes; area and radius are different.

title: The ideal voltmeter
idea: A voltmeter measures the potential difference between two points without drawing current in the ideal limit.
variables: An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance and is connected in parallel across the element.
steps: Choose the two measurement points.
Connect the voltmeter across them, not in series.
Infinite resistance makes its branch current zero.
examplePrompt: A meter is placed across a resistor in a working circuit.
exampleSteps: To leave the branch current unchanged, the meter should draw no extra current.
That corresponds to the ideal infinite-resistance limit.
pitfall: An ideal ammeter has the opposite resistance requirement: zero.

title: The thin-lens equation
idea: A thin lens links object distance, image distance and focal length. Consistent signs are as important as substitution.
variables: With light travelling left to right, measure distances from the optical centre. A real object on the left has u < 0; a convex lens in air has f > 0.
steps: State the sign convention.
Substitute signed u and f, then solve for v.
A positive v is on the outgoing-light side in this convention.
examplePrompt: A convex lens has f = +10 cm and u = −20 cm.
exampleSteps: 1/v = 1/20, so v = +20 cm: a real image on the other side.
pitfall: Do not change the convention partway through the calculation.

title: Lens power and combinations
idea: Optical power is the reciprocal of focal length in metres. For thin lenses in contact, add their signed powers.
variables: Power is in dioptres (D). A converging lens has positive power; a diverging lens has negative power in air.
steps: Convert centimetres to metres before taking a reciprocal.
Keep the sign of each focal length or power.
For thin lenses in contact, add powers rather than focal lengths.
examplePrompt: A +4 D lens and a −1 D lens are in contact.
exampleSteps: Their total power is +4 + (−1) = +3 D.
The combined focal length is 1/3 m, approximately +33 cm.
pitfall: A centimetre-to-metre error changes the numerical power by a factor of 100.

title: An object at the focus
idea: For an ideal thin convex lens, light from an axial object at the front focal point emerges parallel.
variables: An image at infinity means the emerging rays are parallel; they do not meet at a finite image distance.
steps: Place the object at the front principal focus.
Trace two rays through the lens, or substitute u = −f.
The outgoing rays are parallel in the ideal paraxial model.
examplePrompt: A small object is at the front focus of a convex lens.
exampleSteps: The lens equation gives 1/v = 0.
Its image is at infinity, represented by parallel emerging rays.
pitfall: Infinity here is an image location, not infinite brightness or lens power.

title: Images from a concave lens
idea: A concave lens in air diverges light. For a real object, backward extensions of the outgoing rays form a virtual, erect, diminished image.
variables: This statement is for a single thin concave lens in air with a real object. Different incoming beams can change the situation.
steps: Trace an axial ray and a ray parallel to the axis.
Extend the refracted rays backward to find their apparent meeting point.
The apparent image is upright and smaller than the real object.
examplePrompt: A real object is moved closer to a concave lens.
exampleSteps: The lens still produces a virtual, erect, diminished image under these conditions.
The image position and size change, but this image type does not.
pitfall: Do not transfer the convex-lens real-image rule to a diverging lens.

title: Signed magnification
idea: The magnitude of magnification describes size; its sign describes whether the image is erect or inverted.
variables: For a single thin lens in the Cartesian convention, negative m means inversion. |m| > 1 means enlarged; |m| < 1 means diminished.
steps: Identify whether the image is erect or inverted.
Write the absolute size ratio.
Apply the orientation sign separately.
examplePrompt: A lens makes an inverted image three times the object height.
exampleSteps: The size ratio has magnitude 3.
Inversion gives the minus sign: m = −3.
pitfall: Do not use a positive sign for an inverted image just because its size is larger.
